newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian trade says London robustas due up US$50-$100.
newsitem.headline: Asian trade says London robustas due up US$50-$100.

text.p: London robusta futures are due to open US$50-$100 higher later on Wednesday as the market tries to chase an explosive rally in New York arabica futures, Asian coffee dealers said.

"London will react to New York. I think it will be up $100," a senior coffee dealer said. "With the frost season in Brazil coming up, prices are going to shoot up on almost any news. They're having fun in New York."
"London should be $100 up. This is a good time for coffee producers," a dealer for a commodity house in Singapore echoed.
The July LIFFE coffee futures contract regained a toehold above the $2,100 mark on Tuesday, erasing early losses and closing $15 up on the day at $2,101 a tonne.
July arabicas in New York surged to a contract high of 275.00 U.S. cents/lb before closing 17.45 cents up at 274.30 cents/lb as tight supplies of quality arabica beans fired a speculative-led rally.
"I don't know if London will go that crazy, but it should be $70-$100 up. My feeling is that the rise should be closer to $50," a dealer for a U.S. commodity company said.
Traders said sales by Indonesia, whose crop is currently being harvested, and that of Vietnam have been procedding at a steady pace.
"The Indonesians are selling a lot into the market. The only problem I've seen is that deliveries into town have not been as fast as people would want," one trader said.

The price of Indonesia's benchmark Grade 4 coffee, 80 defects, was seen by regional dealers at $1,860/870 a tonne FOB Lampung, against $1,800/850 a tonne on the same basis last week. The price may soon hit $1,900 a tonne, dealers said.
Asian coffee dealers said an expected fall in Indonesian coffee output will only be seen later in the season.
"There seems to be no crop pressure at the moment. A lot of the beans are coming in," a trader said.
Indonesian exporters have said the crop may fall by up to 30 percent this year after rains and strong winds last year pounded coffee trees, stripping them of their flowers.
Most of the trade said coffee exports should be down by about 20-25 percent to around 230,000-270,000 tonnes.
The trade was divided about how many robusta beans the Vietnamese still have available for the market.
One dealer said the Vietnamese should only have about 10,000 tonnes of beans left. Most disagreed.
"They're still holding some beans. My estimate is about 25,000 tonnes," a trader said.
"I think the Vietnamese may even have more than that," another dealer said. "They've been selling at a steady pace to take advantage of the high prices in the market."
Vietnam's key Grade 2 coffee, 8.0 percent black and broken, was quoted by the trade at $1,840/850 a tonne FOB Saigon, up sharply from last week's quote of $1,700/800 a tonne on the same basis.
Trading in the Singapore Commodity Exchange (SICOM) on Tuesday reached a meagre three lots of the July contract which was settled at $1,945 a tonne. The contract was untraded on Monday.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
